items.definition: to talk with someone in order to reach an agreement, especially about a price or a contract
exampleSentences: The two companies negotiated for months before signing the contract.
She negotiated a better salary before accepting the job offer.
It's often possible to negotiate the price of a used car.

items.definition: a statement that you are willing to give, do, or pay something, especially in a business deal
exampleSentences: The buyer made an offer of ten thousand dollars for the equipment.
They rejected our first offer and asked for more.
Her offer to pay half in advance impressed the supplier.

items.definition: a new offer that you make in reply to an offer you think is not good enough
exampleSentences: The seller rejected the first bid and sent a counteroffer.
After some thought, the vendor made a counteroffer of eight thousand dollars.
Their counteroffer was only slightly lower than the original price.

items.definition: something you agree to give or allow in order to end an argument or reach an agreement
exampleSentences: Neither side wanted to make the first concession.
The union made a small concession on working hours.
Offering free delivery was a concession that helped close the sale.

items.definition: the power to influence people or a situation because of an advantage you have
exampleSentences: Having another buyer interested gave her more leverage in the talks.
The supplier had little leverage because it needed the contract badly.
Use your leverage before you reveal your final price.

items.definition: to discuss the price or conditions of something until both sides agree
exampleSentences: Shoppers at the market often bargain over the price.
The two firms bargained hard before reaching a deal.
At a street market, you can often bargain for a lower price.

items.definition: the conditions that people agree to as part of a contract or deal
exampleSentences: Both companies agreed on the terms of the contract.
We need better payment terms before we sign.
The two sides could not agree on the terms of the deal.

items.definition: an agreement in which each side gives up part of what it wants
exampleSentences: After a long discussion, they reached a compromise on the price.
She was willing to compromise on the delivery date.
Good negotiators know when to compromise.

items.definition: a situation in which neither side will change its position, so no agreement is possible
exampleSentences: The talks ended in deadlock after six hours.
A single clause caused a deadlock between the two sides.
They finally broke the deadlock by agreeing to a trial period.

items.definition: an amount taken off the usual price of something
exampleSentences: The supplier offered a ten percent discount for a large order.
We asked for a discount because we were buying in bulk.
Loyal buyers get a discount on their next order.

items.definition: a written statement of the price a company will charge for a job, service, or order
exampleSentences: The vendor sent a detailed quotation for the new equipment.
Ask for a written quotation before making a decision.
Their quotation was surprisingly close to our budget.

items.definition: the difference between the cost of making something and the price it is sold for
exampleSentences: A big discount would cut into our profit margin.
The company works on a thin margin, so every cent counts.
Higher sales volume can make up for a smaller margin.

items.definition: something that encourages you to do something or to work harder
exampleSentences: Free shipping was the incentive that convinced her to buy today.
The company offers incentives for early payment.
A price incentive can speed up a slow negotiation.

items.definition: paid or given before something happens, not afterward
exampleSentences: The supplier asked for fifty percent upfront.
We prefer to pay upfront for a lower price.
An upfront payment showed the buyer was serious.

items.definition: an agreement between two or more people or companies, especially one about buying or selling something
exampleSentences: After three rounds of talks, the two firms finally closed the deal.
We got a good deal on the new laptops because we ordered fifty.
The deal includes free maintenance for the first year.

items.definition: a person or company that sells goods or services
exampleSentences: We compared quotations from three different vendors.
The vendor agreed to lower the price for a bigger order.
Choosing the right vendor can take weeks of negotiation.

items.definition: a company that provides goods or materials to another business
exampleSentences: The supplier raised its prices last quarter.
We asked our supplier for a longer payment period.
Finding a new supplier took several rounds of talks.

items.definition: a written agreement between two or more sides that can be enforced by law
exampleSentences: Both sides signed the contract after weeks of talks.
The contract included a clause about late delivery.
She read every line of the contract before agreeing to it.

items.definition: a single part of a legal document that deals with one particular point
exampleSentences: They added a clause allowing early cancellation.
One clause in the contract worried the buyer.
The lawyer explained each clause before we signed.

items.definition: not able to be changed or discussed
exampleSentences: The delivery date was non-negotiable for the buyer.
Our safety standards are non-negotiable, whatever the price.
He made it clear that the deadline was non-negotiable.

items.definition: the most important point, especially the final amount of profit or loss
exampleSentences: The bottom line is that we need a better price.
A ten percent discount would hurt our bottom line.
Whatever the details, the bottom line has to work for both sides.

items.definition: a balance between two things that you cannot have at the same time
exampleSentences: Lower prices are often a trade-off for slower delivery.
Every negotiation involves some kind of trade-off.
They accepted the trade-off between cost and quality.

items.definition: good for both sides in a deal, not just one
exampleSentences: A flexible delivery date created a win-win outcome for both companies.
Good negotiators look for a win-win solution.
The final deal felt like a true win-win.

items.definition: to make an offer more attractive by adding something extra
exampleSentences: The vendor offered free installation to sweeten the deal.
They sweetened the deal with an extra year of support.
A small discount can sweeten the deal without hurting margins much.

items.definition: to stop being part of a negotiation or deal, usually because the terms are not good enough
exampleSentences: She was ready to walk away if they wouldn't lower the price.
Sometimes the best move in a negotiation is to walk away.
He decided to walk away from the deal when the terms changed.

items.definition: to compromise with someone by moving part of the way toward their position
exampleSentences: Let's meet halfway and split the difference in price.
Neither side would meet halfway at first.
The two companies finally decided to meet halfway on the delivery schedule.

items.definition: to make a final agreement official, often by shaking hands or signing
exampleSentences: A firm handshake sealed the deal.
They needed one more concession to seal the deal.
Signing the contract finally sealed the deal.

items.definition: a rough number or amount that is not exact
exampleSentences: Can you give me a ballpark figure before the formal quotation?
The ballpark figure was much higher than we expected.
A ballpark figure is enough at this early stage.

items.definition: good for both sides involved in an agreement
exampleSentences: They aimed for terms that were mutually beneficial.
A mutually beneficial deal keeps both companies happy.
The partnership proved mutually beneficial for years.

items.definition: to refuse to change your position during a discussion or negotiation
exampleSentences: The union decided to hold firm on the pay increase.
Buyers should hold firm on their maximum price.
She continued to hold firm even when the supplier pushed back.

items.definition: using if-clauses to talk about likely and unlikely outcomes in a negotiation
items.explanationTR:
In negotiations, we use conditional sentences to talk about possible outcomes and their results.

• First conditional (if + present simple, ... will + base verb): a realistic condition and its likely result.
  - If you lower the price, we will sign today.
  - If they refuse the terms, we will look for another supplier.

• Second conditional (if + past simple, ... would + base verb): an unlikely, hypothetical, or unreal condition and its result now or in the future.
  - If I were the buyer, I would ask for a longer warranty.
  - If we had a bigger budget, we would accept your first offer.

• Choose the first conditional when the condition is realistic or still open to negotiation. Choose the second conditional when the condition is unlikely, imaginary, or you want to sound more polite and less direct.

• In the second conditional, 'were' is used for all subjects after 'if' in careful, formal English: If I were you, I would negotiate harder.

• Both types use a comma when the if-clause comes first, but no comma when it comes second: We will sign today if you lower the price.

questions.prompt: If you ---- us a ten percent discount, we will sign the contract today.
options: give
gave
will give
giving
had given
questions.explanationTR: The first conditional needs the present simple after 'if' for a realistic condition; 'will sign' in the main clause confirms this is a first conditional sentence.

questions.prompt: If I ---- you, I would ask for a longer payment period.
options: am
will be
were
was being
have been
questions.explanationTR: This is a hypothetical second conditional, so the if-clause uses the past simple, and 'were' is the standard form for all subjects; 'am' is present tense and does not fit the unreal, hypothetical situation.

questions.prompt: We ---- the deal if they don't meet our minimum price.
options: not sign
will not sign
would not sign
will not signed
not signing
questions.explanationTR: The if-clause uses the present simple ('don't meet'), so this is a first conditional and the main clause needs 'will' plus the base verb; 'would not sign' wrongly shifts to the second conditional pattern.

questions.prompt: If the supplier ---- more flexible, we would consider a longer contract.
options: is
will be
has been
were
being
questions.explanationTR: 'Would consider' in the main clause signals a second conditional, so the if-clause needs the past form 'were', not the present tense 'is', which would suggest a first conditional instead.

options: If they didn't lower their price
If they will not lower their price
If they wouldn't lower their price
If they not lower their price
If they don't lower their price
questions.explanationTR: 'Will lose' in the main clause shows a first conditional, so the if-clause must use the present simple 'don't lower'; the other options wrongly use past forms or 'will' inside the if-clause.

questions.prompt: If we had more leverage, we ---- for a better deal.
options: would push
will push
push
pushed
would pushed
questions.explanationTR: The if-clause 'had more leverage' is a past-simple hypothetical, so the main clause needs 'would' plus the base verb 'push'; 'will push' incorrectly mixes in the first conditional pattern.

questions.prompt: Choose the sentence that correctly uses the first conditional.
options: If you signed today, we will include free installation.
If you will sign today, we include free installation.
If you sign today, we will include free installation.
If you signing today, we include free installation.
If you sign today, we would include free installation.
questions.explanationTR: The first conditional needs the present simple in the if-clause ('sign') and 'will' plus the base verb in the main clause ('will include'); the other options use the wrong tense in one of the two clauses.

questions.prompt: If they ---- their offer, we would seriously consider it.
options: improve
will improve
have improved
improving
improved
questions.explanationTR: 'Would seriously consider' shows this is a second conditional, so the if-clause needs the past simple 'improved'; the present form 'improve' belongs to the first conditional, and 'have improved' does not fit the would-clause.

items.definition: Seven short dialogues between buyers and sellers, each missing one line

questions.prompt:
Maria: We really like your proposal, but the price is above our budget.
Vendor: I understand. ----
Maria: That would help a lot. Can we also talk about the delivery schedule?
options: We could offer a five percent discount for a longer contract.
I'm afraid the price is completely fixed and simply cannot be changed no matter what.
Then perhaps you should look at another vendor instead.
Our delivery schedule is also above your budget limit.
The contract was already signed, so nothing can change now.
questions.explanationTR: Maria's reply 'That would help a lot' only makes sense if the vendor just offered a concrete concession, such as a discount; the other replies close the conversation instead of moving it forward.

questions.prompt:
Daniel: Before you prepare a formal quotation, could you tell me roughly what this would cost?
Supplier: ----
Daniel: A ballpark figure is fine for now. We just need to check it against our budget.
options: The other vendors are clearly overcharging you for the very same equipment.
I can give you a ballpark figure now, but the final price may change.
Your budget is not really our concern, I'm afraid.
We signed the contract with you last week.
Our delivery team can start work next Monday.
questions.explanationTR: Daniel asks for a rough price and then says 'A ballpark figure is fine for now,' so the supplier must have offered an approximate number; the other replies ignore his question or talk about a contract that has not been made yet.

questions.prompt:
Priya: If we sign a three-year contract, will you lower the price per unit?
Tomas: ----
Priya: That sounds fair. Let's put it in writing.
options: No, the price stays exactly the same no matter how long or short the contract eventually runs for us.
We would need you to pay double the amount upfront instead.
Yes, with a three-year contract we could lower the unit price by five percent.
That's not possible; our margin is already at zero percent.
We could extend the contract to five years at the same price.
questions.explanationTR: Priya calls the reply 'fair,' which only fits an answer that actually offers a lower price tied to the longer contract; the other options either refuse outright or ignore her question about the price per unit.

questions.prompt:
Wei: We're at a bit of a deadlock. Neither side wants to move on the delivery date.
Fatima: ----
Wei: Meeting halfway on the schedule works for us.
options: Let's just cancel the whole deal right now without any further discussion.
I absolutely refuse to discuss the delivery date any further at all.
The delivery date really isn't part of this negotiation at all.
What if we split the difference and agree on a date in the middle?
You should just accept our original date without any changes.
questions.explanationTR: Wei's response 'meeting halfway... works for us' directly matches a proposal to split the difference; the other options either end the negotiation or refuse to compromise.

questions.prompt:
Grace: This offer is close, but the payment terms are still a problem for us.
Marco: ----
Grace: An extra thirty days would make this much easier for us to accept.
options: The payment terms are completely non-negotiable, I'm afraid, no matter what you offer.
You should really just pay everything entirely upfront instead.
We could reduce the total contract length by exactly thirty days.
Our payment terms honestly have nothing at all to do with this.
We could extend the payment period by thirty days if that helps.
questions.explanationTR: Grace's reply mentions 'an extra thirty days,' so Marco's line must be the offer to extend the payment period by that amount; calling the terms non-negotiable would make Grace's positive reply illogical.

questions.prompt:
Hassan: Before we go further, what's your bottom line on this deal?
Layla: ----
Hassan: Then let's see if we can find a number close to that.
options: I honestly have absolutely no idea at all what our bottom line even is right now.
We can't accept less than twelve thousand dollars for the full order.
There is no bottom line at all; any price is completely fine.
That question is really not appropriate in a negotiation like this.
Our bottom line apparently changes every single day, unfortunately.
questions.explanationTR: Hassan's follow-up about finding 'a number close to that' only makes sense if Layla just named a concrete minimum price; the other replies avoid answering the direct question.

questions.prompt:
Sofia: We'd like to close this deal today if possible.
Renzo: ----
Sofia: Great, let's sign the contract this afternoon then.
options: I really need at least another full month to think it over carefully.
We're actually walking away from this negotiation completely, effective immediately.
If you agree to the current terms, we can seal the deal today too.
Let's just postpone this whole decision until next quarter instead.
I haven't even received your official offer yet, unfortunately.
questions.explanationTR: Sofia's enthusiastic reply about signing 'this afternoon' fits only an answer that also agrees to close today; the other options involve delay or withdrawal, which would contradict her response.
